sources.note: Screens 9 and 25 are the Android system permission dialog drawn over the app; the tester recorded their 6 marked buttons as detection false positives, did not judge them, and did not show them to the personas. Screens 29 and 30 are out-of-app (Google Play billing sheet, Chrome) and carry no marked elements. All four personas ran. Two elements (screen13-a2, screen15-a2) carry a split persona-issue classification (see classification_basis).

screen1-a1.appearance: three horizontal lines of decreasing length
screen1-a1.description: three stacked lines control in the top-left corner of the toolbar

tester.deciding_evidence: tapping the hamburger opened the side navigation panel, exactly what the convention promises

personas.expectation: It opens the side menu with the list of sections.
personas.cue: The three-line icon. It is the standard menu glyph, and screen 2 shows the menu it opens.
personas.why: It is a standard menu symbol in a fixed position at the top left on every main screen. I know what it does.

personas.expectation: I believe it opens a list of other places in the application, but that is a guess.
personas.cue: Nothing but the three lines themselves; there is no word beside them.
personas.why: Three lines are not a word. I cannot be certain what they do, and I cannot carry the answer from one screen to the next; each time I would have to press it to find out.
personas.solution: Put the word 'Menu' under or beside the three lines.

personas.expectation: It opens the app's main menu, the list of places I can go.
personas.cue: The three stacked lines. I have learned that shape means a menu, and it sits where menus usually sit.
personas.why: This is one picture I do know by now. I would say 'tap menu' or tap it and expect the side list to open.

personas.expectation: Opens the side menu with the rest of the app in it.
personas.cue: The three-lines picture - every app I use has it there.
personas.why: I know this one without thinking.

screen1-a2.appearance: ghost outline with two dots for eyes
screen1-a2.description: ghost outline glyph in the top-right corner of the toolbar

tester.deciding_evidence: no label, tooltip or adjacent copy exists before the tap, and the ghost glyph is not a convention; the explanation is shown only after the user has already switched modes
tester.recommendation: put a visible word beside or under the glyph, e.g. 'Incognito' (or 'Private chat'), so the mode is named before it is switched on

personas.expectation: I do not know. A ghost is not an action. Maybe something to do with hiding, or something 'spooky'. I cannot tell from this screen.
personas.cue: Nothing. There is no word next to it; it is a picture of a ghost.
personas.why: A ghost represents an idea, not a thing I can name as an action. Nothing on this screen tells me what pressing it does.
personas.solution: Put a text label next to it, for example 'Incognito chat', or at least show the words when I hold my finger on it.

personas.expectation: I have no idea. A ghost means nothing to me in a telephone.
personas.cue: Nothing. There is only the drawing of a ghost, and no word.
personas.why: It is a picture I have never learned and cannot learn. I would not press it, or if I did I would not know what I had done.
personas.solution: Replace the ghost with plain words that say what it does, written on the button itself.

personas.expectation: I do not know. It is a small ghost face. I cannot connect a ghost to anything I would want to do in a chat app.
personas.cue: Only the picture of the ghost. There are no words next to it at all.
personas.why: I cannot recognise what a ghost is supposed to stand for, and nothing on the screen names it. I would not press it, because I could not predict where it would take me, and I could not ask for it by voice because I do not know what to call it.
personas.solution: Put a word under it or beside it that says what it does, in plain terms. If it starts a private chat, say 'Private chat'.

personas.expectation: Maybe some kind of hidden or private chat? Or it could be something fun that pops up. I honestly would have to press it to find out.
personas.cue: Only the ghost picture. No word anywhere near it.
personas.why: A ghost could mean a lot of things - private, hidden, deleted, a game. Up in the corner with no word, I either skip it or tap it just to see, and then I've lost my train of thought.
personas.solution: Put one word under or beside it, like 'Private chat', so I know before I tap.

screen1-a2.recommendation: put a visible word beside or under the glyph, e.g. 'Incognito' (or 'Private chat'), so the mode is named before it is switched on

screen1-a3.appearance: "Upgrade to Pro" beside the banner text "Get more with Claude Pro"
screen1-a3.description: 'Upgrade to Pro' link at the right of the grey banner above the typing box

tester.deciding_evidence: the link opened the plan screen it names

personas.expectation: It takes me to a page where I can pay for the Pro plan.
personas.cue: The words 'Upgrade to Pro' and the strip text 'Get more with Claude Pro'.
personas.why: The text says literally what it does.

personas.expectation: It would take me to a page asking me to pay for a better version of the service.
personas.cue: The words 'Upgrade to Pro' and 'Get more with Claude Pro' beside them.
personas.why: 'Upgrade' is an ordinary word. I know it means paying for more.

personas.expectation: It takes me to a page where I can pay for the Pro version.
personas.cue: The words 'Upgrade to Pro' and the line beside them, 'Get more with Claude Pro'.
personas.why: The words say exactly what will happen.

personas.expectation: Takes me to pay for the Pro version.
personas.cue: The words 'Upgrade to Pro' and 'Get more with Claude Pro' next to them.
personas.why: It says exactly what it does.

screen1-a4.description: text entry box at the bottom of the screen

tester.deciding_evidence: the placeholder survives focus and names the job; it is replaced only by the user's own message, with a send arrow appearing

personas.expectation: I type my message to Claude.
personas.cue: The placeholder text 'Chat with Claude...'.
personas.why: It is a text box with a literal instruction in it.

personas.expectation: I type my question or my message to the assistant here.
personas.cue: The words 'Chat with Claude…' written inside the box.
personas.why: I understand it is where I write. I notice the grey words sit inside the box and will vanish when I begin, but what I am writing is my own message, so I do not lose the thread.

personas.expectation: The question or message I want to send to Claude.
personas.cue: The grey words 'Chat with Claude...' inside the box.
personas.why: It is a plain typing box and the words inside it tell me what it is for.

personas.expectation: My question or message to Claude.
personas.cue: The grey words 'Chat with Claude...' inside the box.
personas.why: Clear - I type here and talk to it.

screen1-a5.appearance: plus sign in a grey circle
screen1-a5.description: plus sign in a grey circle at the left of the typing bar
screen1-a5.issue_source: classified by se-tester from persona feedback
screen1-a5.classification_basis: Amy: cue "Only the plus sign. The 'Add to chat' sheet on screen 6 suggests this is what opens it, but nothing on this screen says so."; why "A plus by itself can mean several things: add a file, add a new chat, add a project. The same plus is used on 'New chat' and 'New project', where it means something else."; solution "Put a word next to it, like 'Attach' or 'Add to chat'." (opinion after testing: softened) | Gopal: cue "Only the plus sign. No word."; why "A plus sign means 'add', but add what? Nothing on the screen tells me, and I would have to press it to find out every time."; solution "Write 'Add a file or photo' (or whatever it adds) next to the plus sign." (opinion after testing: softened) | Kwame: cue "Only the plus sign."; why "A plus means 'add', but add what? It could equally be a new chat or an attachment. I would read the area over and over and still not be able to commit."; solution "A short word next to it, such as 'Attach' or 'Add file', so I know which kind of adding it is." (opinion after testing: softened) — read together, this describes being given something (a word, a picture or a value) that did not tell them enough.

tester.deciding_evidence: the plus opened the 'Add to chat' sheet, as the add convention promises

personas.expectation: It adds something to the message, probably an attachment. It could also mean 'new chat', because the New chat button in the menu uses the same plus.
personas.cue: Only the plus sign. The 'Add to chat' sheet on screen 6 suggests this is what opens it, but nothing on this screen says so.
personas.why: A plus by itself can mean several things: add a file, add a new chat, add a project. The same plus is used on 'New chat' and 'New project', where it means something else.
personas.solution: Put a word next to it, like 'Attach' or 'Add to chat'.

personas.expectation: It adds something, but I cannot say what — a new chat, a picture, a file?
personas.cue: Only the plus sign. No word.
personas.why: A plus sign means 'add', but add what? Nothing on the screen tells me, and I would have to press it to find out every time.
personas.solution: Write 'Add a file or photo' (or whatever it adds) next to the plus sign.

personas.expectation: It adds something, but I am not sure what: perhaps a file or picture to the message, perhaps a whole new chat.
personas.cue: Only the plus sign.
personas.why: A plus means 'add', but add what? It could equally be a new chat or an attachment. I would read the area over and over and still not be able to commit.
personas.solution: A short word next to it, such as 'Attach' or 'Add file', so I know which kind of adding it is.

personas.expectation: Adds something to my message - a photo or a file, probably.
personas.cue: The plus sign sitting right next to where I type, like in my messaging apps.
personas.why: I'm not 100% sure, but it's where every chat app puts the 'add a picture' button, so I'd tap it without worrying.

screen1-a5.disagreement_note: the tester cleared the glyph under the common-icon exemption (the plus opened the 'Add to chat' sheet, as the add convention promises); Amy, Gopal, Kwame did not read the convention — Amy: "A plus by itself can mean several things: add a file, add a new chat, add a project."
screen1-a5.recommendation: persona solution — Amy: "Put a word next to it, like 'Attach' or 'Add to chat'." | Gopal: "Write 'Add a file or photo' (or whatever it adds) next to the plus sign." | Kwame: "A short word next to it, such as 'Attach' or 'Add file', so I know which kind of adding it is."

screen1-a6.description: pill in the typing bar with the words 'Haiku 4.5'

tester.deciding_evidence: the purpose ('choose the model') is disclosed only by the sheet the tap opens; the pill's face is a product name a first-time user cannot interpret
tester.recommendation: show the purpose on the pill, e.g. 'Model: Haiku 4.5 ▾', or a caption 'Choose model'

personas.expectation: I think it changes some setting, maybe a version. 'Haiku' is a kind of Japanese poem, so literally I would think it writes poems. The number suggests it is a product or model name.
personas.cue: The words 'Haiku 4.5'. Nothing says what kind of thing Haiku is.
personas.why: The label is a name that is a metaphor. Nothing on this screen says it is the model picker.
personas.solution: Add the word 'Model', for example 'Model: Haiku 4.5'.

personas.expectation: I have no idea. A haiku is a Japanese poem. Perhaps it writes a poem for me?
personas.cue: The words 'Haiku 4.5', which are a name, not an instruction.
personas.why: It is an invented name with a number. I cannot learn what it stands for, so it is a wall to me.
personas.solution: Say what it does in ordinary words, for example 'Choose how the assistant answers: quick or careful', and keep that wording the same everywhere.

personas.expectation: I am guessing it lets me change some setting or version, because it has a number on it. A haiku is a short poem, so part of me wonders whether it makes Claude write poems.
personas.cue: The words 'Haiku 4.5'. They are a name, not an instruction.
personas.why: The words are there, but they do not say what the button does. 'Haiku' has a meaning I already know, and it is the wrong one here, so I get stuck on the ambiguity.
personas.solution: A small label that says what it is, such as 'Model: Haiku 4.5', or a down-arrow so I know it opens a choice.

personas.expectation: No real idea - some kind of style or setting? 'Haiku' makes me think of a short poem, so maybe it makes the answers short?
personas.cue: The words 'Haiku 4.5', which don't tell me what it is.
personas.why: The word is a name, not an instruction. Nothing tells me it's something I can change, or what changing it does. I'd probably ignore it.
personas.solution: Show that it's a chooser - a small down-arrow and a word like 'Model:' in front - so I know I can pick something here.

screen1-a6.recommendation: show the purpose on the pill, e.g. 'Model: Haiku 4.5 ▾', or a caption 'Choose model'

screen1-a7.appearance: microphone outline in a grey circle
screen1-a7.description: microphone outline in a grey circle, second from the right in the typing bar
screen1-a7.issue_source: classified by se-tester from persona feedback
screen1-a7.classification_basis: Kwame: cue "The microphone picture. I use speech recognition, so I know that picture well."; why "On its own I would be fairly confident. But right next to it is a second button that also looks to do with sound, and I cannot tell which of the two is for dictating and which is for something else. With two voice-looking buttons side by side I lose my certainty."; solution "Words under each of the two buttons that make the difference plain, for example 'Dictate' under this one and 'Voice conversation' under the other." (opinion after testing: softened) — read together, this describes being given something (a word, a picture or a value) that did not tell them enough.

tester.deciding_evidence: the microphone opened a voice-dictation intro, matching the convention

personas.expectation: I speak and my words are typed into the text box.
personas.cue: The microphone picture. A microphone is a real object I can name.
personas.why: A microphone means speaking. That part is clear to me.

personas.expectation: I would speak into the telephone instead of typing.
personas.cue: The drawing of a microphone, which I have known all my life.
personas.why: A microphone is a familiar object; it means talking.

personas.expectation: It lets me speak instead of typing, so my words are turned into text.
personas.cue: The microphone picture. I use speech recognition, so I know that picture well.
personas.why: On its own I would be fairly confident. But right next to it is a second button that also looks to do with sound, and I cannot tell which of the two is for dictating and which is for something else. With two voice-looking buttons side by side I lose my certainty.
personas.solution: Words under each of the two buttons that make the difference plain, for example 'Dictate' under this one and 'Voice conversation' under the other.

personas.expectation: Lets me say my message out loud instead of typing it.
personas.cue: The microphone picture right next to the typing box.
personas.why: Microphone next to a text box means talk instead of type. Easy.

screen1-a7.disagreement_note: the tester cleared the glyph under the common-icon exemption (the microphone opened a voice-dictation intro, matching the convention); Kwame did not read the convention — Kwame: "On its own I would be fairly confident."
screen1-a7.recommendation: persona solution — Kwame: "Words under each of the two buttons that make the difference plain, for example 'Dictate' under this one and 'Voice conversation' under the other."

screen1-a8.appearance: white vertical bars of varying height in a black circle
screen1-a8.description: round black button with white vertical bars at the right end of the typing bar

tester.deciding_evidence: verification found no visible text in any reachable state and the glyph is not a convention; the behavioural tap could not be run, so the verdict is provisional
tester.recommendation: add a visible label such as 'Talk' or 'Voice chat' under or beside the button, distinct from the microphone

personas.expectation: Something with voice. Maybe a spoken conversation. But it sits where the Send button usually is, so it might also send.
personas.cue: Only the bars, which look like a sound wave. Nothing says how it is different from the microphone next to it.
personas.why: It is a picture of a sound, not of an action. It sits right next to a microphone, so I cannot tell which one is for dictation and which one is for something else. It is also the biggest, darkest button, in the place where Send usually is.
personas.solution: Label both: for example 'Dictate' under the microphone and 'Voice mode' under the bars.

personas.expectation: I have no idea. Perhaps it sends my message, perhaps it is to do with sound.
personas.cue: Nothing. Only some upright lines of different heights.
personas.why: I do not recognise this picture, and it sits right beside the microphone, so I could not tell the two apart or know which one to use.
personas.solution: Put a plain word on it — 'Send' or 'Talk', whichever it is.

personas.expectation: Something with voice or sound. It could be a spoken conversation, or it might be the send button, because the bottom right is where send usually is.
personas.cue: Only the picture of the vertical lines, like a sound wave, and its position where a send button would normally be.
personas.why: I cannot choose between two readings: send my message, or start talking. They are very different actions, and the one next to it also looks like sound. I would hesitate here every time.
personas.solution: A word on or under it saying what it does, and keep a separate, clearly named send button.

personas.expectation: Something with voice again - maybe a spoken conversation where Claude talks back? Or maybe it's send?
personas.cue: The sound-wave lines, and that it's bigger and black like a main button.
personas.why: There's already a microphone right beside it, so two voice-looking buttons side by side and I can't tell which is which. Being the big black one, I half expect it to be 'send'.
personas.solution: Put a short word under each - like 'Dictate' and 'Talk' - or make the difference obvious in the picture.

screen1-a8.recommendation: add a visible label such as 'Talk' or 'Voice chat' under or beside the button, distinct from the microphone

screen2-a1.appearance: dimmed grey strip along the right screen edge, no symbol of its own
screen2-a1.description: dimmed grey strip along the right edge beside the open side panel; the ghost glyph of the screen beneath shows through it

tester.deciding_evidence: the only visible thing in the strip is a glyph from the covered screen, and tapping it closes the panel instead of doing that glyph's job
tester.recommendation: dim the covered screen enough that its controls do not read as live, or give the panel its own visible close control (an X or 'Close') at the top

personas.expectation: The side menu closes and I go back to the screen behind it. But the strip also contains a greyed-out icon, so I am not sure whether that icon gets pressed instead.
personas.cue: Nothing visible. It is just a grey shaded area. I know from other apps that tapping outside a side menu closes it.
personas.why: There is no visible button, no X and no words. I have to rely on a habit from other apps. And there is an icon from the screen behind showing through it, which makes me unsure what my tap hits.
personas.solution: Put a visible close button (an X or the word 'Close') on the menu itself.

personas.expectation: I do not know that it is something to press. If I pressed it, perhaps the list on the left would go away, but that is a guess.
personas.cue: Nothing. It is a greyed-out slice of the screen behind; there is no word on it.
personas.why: I would not think of this as a button. And the little picture showing in it looks like a button of its own, so I might press that thinking I was pressing something else.
personas.solution: Give the list a clear 'Close' button with the word on it.

personas.expectation: I think tapping the grey part closes the menu and takes me back to the screen underneath.
personas.cue: Nothing written. Only that the screen behind is greyed out and still partly visible.
personas.why: There is nothing drawn there to press; I would only know from habit that tapping outside closes a menu. I can also see a bit of the old screen's buttons through the grey, and I would worry I was pressing those instead.
personas.solution: A clear close button or a 'Back' word at the top of the menu, so I do not have to guess that the grey area is a button.

personas.expectation: Closes the menu and takes me back to the screen underneath.
personas.cue: The screen behind is greyed out, which is what happens when a menu is open on top.
personas.why: Tapping the dark bit to get out of a menu is normal. I'd do it without thinking.

screen2-a1.recommendation: dim the covered screen enough that its controls do not read as live, or give the panel its own visible close control (an X or 'Close') at the top

screen2-a2.appearance: "Claude" (the product's name, set as a title)
screen2-a2.description: large word 'Claude' at the top of the side panel

tester.deciding_evidence: the title is actionable and starts a new chat, which the product name gives no hint of
tester.recommendation: make the title non-interactive, or label the action it performs (e.g. 'Home' / 'New chat')

personas.expectation: I do not know. It looks like a heading or a logo. Maybe it takes me to the start screen, maybe nothing happens.
personas.cue: The word 'Claude', which is the name of the app, not an action.
personas.why: It is drawn as a title, not as a button. The name of the app tells me nothing about what pressing it does.
personas.solution: If it is a button, say what it does, for example 'Home'. If it is not a button, it should not react.

personas.expectation: I would expect nothing to happen; it looks like the name at the top of the page. Perhaps it takes me to the start.
personas.cue: Only the word 'Claude', which reads as a title.
personas.why: It looks like a heading, not a button. I cannot tell that pressing it does anything, or what.
personas.solution: If it takes me to the start page, say 'Home' or 'Start page' on it.

personas.expectation: I do not expect anything. It looks like the name of the app, a title. If it does something, perhaps it takes me home.
personas.cue: Only the word 'Claude', written like a heading.
personas.why: It reads as a title, not a button. I cannot tell that it does anything, and if it does, nothing says what.
personas.solution: If it takes me home, say 'Home'. If it does nothing, it should not behave like a button.

personas.expectation: I don't know if it does anything - it looks like the name of the app. Maybe it takes me home?
personas.cue: Just the word 'Claude' in big letters, like a heading.
personas.why: It looks like a title, not a button, so I wouldn't expect it to be pressable. If it does something I'd never find out.
personas.solution: If it's a way home, make it look like a button or say 'Home'. If it's just the name, it shouldn't do anything.

screen2-a2.recommendation: make the title non-interactive, or label the action it performs (e.g. 'Home' / 'New chat')

screen2-a3.description: 'Chats' row with a speech-bubbles glyph in the side panel

tester.deciding_evidence: opened the Chats list it names

personas.expectation: It shows the list of my past chats.
personas.cue: The word 'Chats' and the speech bubble picture.
personas.why: Literal word, and the icon shows a real thing (speech bubbles).

personas.expectation: It would show me my earlier conversations.
personas.cue: The word 'Chats'.
personas.why: 'Chats' is an ordinary word, and the words are there beside the picture.

personas.expectation: It shows me my earlier conversations.
personas.cue: The word 'Chats' and the two speech bubbles.
personas.why: The word is plain and the picture agrees with it.

personas.expectation: Shows me my old conversations.
personas.cue: The word 'Chats' and the speech bubbles.
personas.why: Clear word, clear picture.

screen2-a4.description: 'Projects' row with a stacked-tray glyph in the side panel

tester.deciding_evidence: opened the Projects screen, which also explains what a project is

personas.expectation: It shows my projects.
personas.cue: The word 'Projects'. The Projects screen confirms it: 'Create a project to organize chats'.
personas.why: The word is literal. I do not understand the icon (it looks like a stacked tray or a bin), but the word is enough.

personas.expectation: It would open a page of my projects.
personas.cue: The word 'Projects'.
personas.why: It is a plain word and it is written out; I would expect a page called Projects.

personas.expectation: It takes me to a page called Projects, where things are organised into projects.
personas.cue: The word 'Projects'.
personas.why: I am not certain what a 'project' means in this app, but I am certain where I will end up: a page called Projects. That is enough for me to press it.

personas.expectation: Shows my projects - groups of work I've set up.
personas.cue: The word 'Projects'.
personas.why: It says what it is.

screen2-a5.description: 'Code' row with a </> glyph in the side panel

tester.deciding_evidence: the row leads to a paid-product upgrade page; neither the product nor the paywall is conveyed by the single word 'Code'
tester.recommendation: name the destination, e.g. 'Claude Code (coding assistant) — Pro'

personas.expectation: It goes to an area for writing or running code.
personas.cue: The word 'Code' and the </> symbol, which I know from programming.
personas.why: Literal word and a symbol I use every day.

personas.expectation: Something to do with a code — to me as a lawyer that is a body of law, but I suspect here it means computer programming. I do not know which.
personas.cue: The word 'Code' and a symbol I do not recognise.
personas.why: The word is familiar but it has two meanings, and nothing on the screen tells me which one is meant.
personas.solution: Say 'Computer programming' or 'Write computer code' instead of the single word.

personas.expectation: Something to do with computer programming, perhaps writing code with Claude. It could also mean a code I have to enter, like a verification code.
personas.cue: The word 'Code' and the </> picture, which I know from my work means programming.
personas.why: One short word with two ordinary meanings. The picture tips me towards programming, but I still read it twice to be sure.
personas.solution: A few more words, for example 'Code with Claude'.

personas.expectation: Somewhere for writing computer code. Not really for me, but I get what it is.
personas.cue: The word 'Code' and the pointy brackets.
personas.why: I know enough to know it's the coding part, and I can skip it.

screen2-a5.recommendation: name the destination, e.g. 'Claude Code (coding assistant) — Pro'

screen2-a6.description: 'Artifacts' row with a shapes glyph in the side panel

tester.deciding_evidence: neither the row nor the screen it opens explains the term
tester.recommendation: rename or caption it in plain words, e.g. 'Artifacts — documents, code and designs Claude made for you'

personas.expectation: It goes to a list of 'artifacts'. I do not know what an artifact is here. Literally an artifact is an object from archaeology, or a build output in programming.
personas.cue: The word 'Artifacts' and an abstract shape icon. The Artifacts screen only says 'Artifacts you've had with Claude will show up here', which does not define it.
personas.why: The word is not literal in this app, and the icon is abstract shapes. I know it is a section, but not what is in it.
personas.solution: Say what an artifact is, in one plain line under the word, for example 'Documents and code Claude made for you'.

personas.expectation: I have no idea. Artifacts are old objects in a museum.
personas.cue: The word 'Artifacts', which in ordinary speech means old objects.
personas.why: The word does not mean anything useful to me in this setting, and I cannot learn a new meaning for it.
personas.solution: Use ordinary words describing what is kept there, for example 'Things the assistant made for you'.

personas.expectation: I have no idea. An artifact to me is an old object in a museum. I cannot think what it means in a chat app.
personas.cue: The word 'Artifacts' and a picture of overlapping shapes, which does not help me.
personas.why: The word has a meaning I know, and it clearly is not the meaning here, so I cannot commit to anything. The shapes picture adds nothing I can recognise.
personas.solution: Use plain words for what is kept there, or add a short line under it, for example 'Things Claude made for you'.

personas.expectation: Honestly not sure - old things? Stuff Claude has made for me?
personas.cue: Only the word 'Artifacts' and a picture of little shapes, which doesn't help.
personas.why: 'Artifacts' sounds like a museum. The shapes don't explain it. I'd have to open it to find out what it even is.
personas.solution: A few words under it, like 'Things Claude made for you', would do it.

screen2-a6.recommendation: rename or caption it in plain words, e.g. 'Artifacts — documents, code and designs Claude made for you'

screen2-a7.description: orange circle with the letters 'AC' at the bottom-left of the side panel
